about: Anoria: 150 more cards from real history, found only in packs (a draft for Tim to read; nothing in the game loads this file yet). cards: one object per card, with the fields of cards.js (key, n, t, f, c, m, reg, era, y, k, arr, insp, from) and of text.js (cap, ll, tx, fact, say, art; links holds the card's LINKS sentences as 'source>key'). src is the reference page for the card's dates, fact and links. Wikipedia could not be opened from the session that wrote the cards, so each card was checked through web search, which quotes Wikipedia and other pages; src2 is a second page the search quoted in support. sure is true when the search confirmed the card's dates, its fact and every link sentence, and false when it did not return one of them; check says what was not returned, or what the sources disagree about. Picture briefs (art) were written from memory and get the usual audit before any art is made. threads: named lines to collect, shaped like THREADS in cards.js. threadAdds: new cards that belong in a line cards.js already has. existing: links the new cards could give to cards already in the game (each needs a line in FROM or insp, and its sentence in LINKS). merge: what the merge has to do that is not copying. Check with: node scripts/anoria/check-set-150.js

cards.fact: The Greeks counted him the first of their thinkers to explain the world by nature and not by the moods of the gods. One winter, the story goes, he foresaw a great crop of olives, hired every olive press in town, and made a fortune to show that a philosopher could be rich if he cared to be.
cards.art: Thales of Miletus about 590 BC, in the story Aristotle tells of the olive presses: a lean Ionian Greek of about thirty-five with a short dark beard and long hair bound with a band, in a long linen tunic and a wool cloak thrown over one shoulder, leaning at his ease with one arm over the great wooden beam of an olive press in a stone press-house, smiling a little, a small tally stick in his other hand. In front of him a line of farmers waits with baskets heaped with black olives, and the first of them is counting coins into the hand of a clerk. Oil runs from the stone press bed into a jar. Seen from the doorway, from the waist up, his face in the upper right. Archaic Greece: a beam press weighted with stones, not a screw press; no Roman togas, no scrolls of paper. Keep the top left corner dim rafters.

links.@library>euclid: Euclid taught and wrote in Alexandria in the years when its Library was being founded.

cards.tx: Scholar: you draw a card when he arrives.
cards.fact: His Elements builds the whole of geometry, step by step, from a handful of plain starting points. It was copied, printed and taught from for more than two thousand years.
cards.art: Euclid about 300 BC in a shaded colonnade at Alexandria, teaching the first proof of his Elements: a spare Greek man of about fifty with a short grey beard, in a plain wool cloak, seated on a stone bench with a papyrus roll held open between his two hands, reading the next step aloud and glancing over the top of the roll. On the paving at his feet a young pupil kneels, swinging a cord pegged at one end to draw the second of two crossing circles in chalk, the triangle between them already ruled. Two more pupils lean in. The bright harbour shows between the columns. Seen from the pupil's side, low, so that Euclid's face and the roll are in the upper right. Nobody knows his face, so he is an ordinary Greek scholar of his day: no long white beard, no metal compasses with a hinge, no bound books. Keep the top left corner plain column and shadow.
cards.check: The search did not return that he worked in Alexandria under the first Ptolemy, or how long the Elements was taught from. Both are standard, written from memory.

links.@library>eratosthenes: Eratosthenes was the chief librarian of the Library of Alexandria.
links.archimedes>eratosthenes: Archimedes addressed his book The Method to his friend Eratosthenes.

cards.cap: Cyrene and Alexandria, c. 276 to c. 194 BC
cards.tx: Scholar: you draw a card when he arrives.
cards.fact: He worked out the distance around the Earth from the length of a shadow in Alexandria at noon on midsummer's day, when the Sun stood straight overhead in a town far to the south. His answer was close to the true one.
cards.art: Eratosthenes at noon on midsummer's day about 240 BC, measuring the Earth from a courtyard in Alexandria: a Greek scholar of about thirty-five, clean-shaven, in a light linen tunic with a cloak over one arm, down on one knee beside a bronze sundial bowl set on a low pillar, a hollow half-sphere with an upright pin at its centre. He is marking the tip of the pin's short shadow on the inside of the bowl with a reed pen, squinting against the glare, and his other hand shades his eyes. A boy holds an inkpot and a wax tablet. The sun is almost straight overhead, so every shadow in the white courtyard is small and sharp. Seen from the far side of the bowl, his face in the upper right. Ptolemaic Alexandria: no telescope, no globe, no glass lenses. Keep the top left corner bare sunlit wall.

cards.tx: Inspiring: your other Figures here get +1 Might.
cards.fact: He and his school taught that illness has natural causes, and that a doctor should watch the patient closely and note what happens day by day. Many new doctors still take an oath that carries his name.
cards.art: Hippocrates on the island of Kos about 400 BC, examining a patient in the open air: an old man with a bald crown and a short white beard, as the ancient busts named for him show, in a plain cloak that leaves one shoulder bare, bending with his ear laid flat against the bare back of a fisherman who sits on a stool, listening to the man's breathing with his eyes shut and one hand raised for quiet. Two students stand by, one with a wax tablet and stylus ready, the other holding a bowl and a sponge. They are in the dappled shade of a huge plane tree in a small harbour town. Seen from the side, from the waist up, the old doctor's head in the upper right. Classical Greece: no serpent staff, no white coat, no surgery or blood. Keep the top left corner leaves and sky.

links.hippocrates>galen: Galen admired Hippocrates above all other doctors and built his own medicine on his ideas.
links.marcus>galen: Galen was physician at the court of the emperor Marcus Aurelius.

cards.tx: Legacy of Hippocrates. Scholar.
cards.fact: He began as doctor to the gladiators of Pergamon, and their wounds taught him how the body is put together. His books were the last word in medicine, in Europe and the Arab world alike, for well over a thousand years.
cards.art: Galen at about thirty, in AD 158, as physician to the gladiators of Pergamon: a slim Greek with short dark curly hair and a trimmed beard, sleeves pushed up, kneeling on the sand-strewn floor of the gladiators' barracks beside a big wounded fighter who sits propped against a pillar. Galen is binding a deep cut on the man's thigh with a strip of linen soaked in wine, pulling the bandage tight with both hands and looking closely at the wound, a bronze instrument case and a flask open beside him. Other gladiators watch from the shadows, their helmets and a net hanging on the wall. Seen from low down, Galen's face and hands in the upper half, right of centre. Roman Asia Minor in the second century: no crowd, no arena, nothing gory. Keep the top left corner plain barracks wall.

cards.tx: When you play a Relic, draw a card.
cards.fact: In 132 he showed the Han court a bronze urn ringed with eight dragons, each holding a ball above an open-mouthed toad. When the ground shook far away one ball dropped, and it is said to have marked an earthquake days before riders brought the news.
cards.art: Zhang Heng, court astronomer of the Han dynasty, about AD 138, at the moment his earthquake urn proves itself: a slender scholar of sixty with a thin grey beard, in a long dark robe with wide sleeves, a sash and the tall lacquered cap of a Han official, standing with one hand raised and his head turned sharply toward a great bronze vessel shaped like a wine jar, as tall as a man. Eight bronze dragon heads point down around its shoulder, each with a ball in its jaws, and eight bronze toads squat below with their mouths open. One ball is in mid-air, falling from a dragon into a toad. Two junior officials have dropped their bamboo slips and stare. A timber hall with red pillars. Seen from across the vessel, Zhang Heng's face in the upper right. Eastern Han China: writing on bamboo slips and silk, no paper books, no chairs. Keep the top left corner dark roof beams.

cards.tx: Scholar: you draw a card when he arrives.
cards.fact: An official of the Han court, he reported to the emperor in 105 a way of making paper from tree bark, hemp, old rags and worn-out fishing nets. Paper of a rougher kind was older, but his was cheap and good enough to write on, and it spread across China.
cards.art: Cai Lun, an official of the imperial workshops of Han China, in AD 105: a beardless man of about fifty, as a palace eunuch was, in a plain belted robe with the sleeves tied back, standing at a wooden vat of grey pulp and lifting out with both hands a square bamboo frame stretched with cloth, water streaming from it and a thin even sheet of wet paper lying on the cloth. He tilts it to the light to judge it. Behind him workers pound bark and rags in a stone mortar, and a long row of the same frames leans against a sunlit wall to dry, each with its pale sheet. Seen from across the vat, from the waist up, his face in the upper right and the dripping frame at the centre. Eastern Han China: no printed pages, no bound books, no writing on the sheets. Keep the top left corner plain wall.
cards.check: His birth year is given as anything from 50 to 62, so the caption gives only his death.

cards.tx: Scholar: you draw a card when he arrives.
cards.fact: His book of 628 is the first we know that treats zero as a number like any other, with rules for adding, taking away and multiplying with it. It speaks of numbers below zero as debts, and numbers above it as fortunes.
cards.art: Brahmagupta at thirty, in AD 628, an astronomer of western India, timing the rising of the Moon from a flat stone roof at dusk: a lean man with his hair tied in a knot on top of his head and a short beard, bare to the waist with a cotton shawl over one shoulder and a wrapped lower cloth. He sits cross-legged, sighting along a straight staff set upright on the parapet toward a huge moon just clearing the horizon, one hand lifted to give the signal. Beside him a pupil watches a water clock, a small copper bowl with a hole in its base slowly sinking in a larger basin, and keeps the count with pebbles. A bundle of palm-leaf pages tied between two boards lies by his knee. Seen from close by on the roof, his face in the upper right. India of the seventh century: palm-leaf pages, no paper books, no telescope, no turban of later centuries. Keep the top left corner darkening sky.
cards.check: The search confirmed the rules for zero and negative numbers; the words debts and fortunes were not returned.

links.brahmagupta>alkhwarizmi: Al-Khwarizmi's star tables follow the Sindhind, an Arabic version of Indian astronomy that is thought to come from Brahmagupta's book, and his own book on Indian numerals taught readers of Arabic to reckon with zero.

cards.tx: Legacy of Brahmagupta. Your Deeds cost 1 less.
cards.fact: His book on solving equations, written in Baghdad about 820, gave algebra its name, from the Arabic word al-jabr in its title. The word algorithm comes from his own name.
cards.art: Al-Khwarizmi about AD 820, on a canal bank outside the round city of Baghdad, putting his new method to work: a scholar of about forty with a full dark beard, in a long plain robe and a neatly wound turban, standing on the raised earth bank with a small wooden writing board held against his chest, a reed pen in his other hand, looking up from his reckoning to call a figure to two surveyors below who are stretching a knotted measuring rope across a field between stakes. A farmer and his brother wait at the field's edge for the answer that will divide their inheritance. Date palms, the canal, and far behind the wall of the city. Seen from the bank, from the waist up, his face in the upper right. Abbasid Iraq: no chalkboard of modern symbols, no x and y, no Ottoman dress. Keep the top left corner pale sky.
cards.check: That the Sindhind comes from Brahmagupta's book is generally presumed, not proven; the link says so.

links.@silk>xuanzang: Xuanzang left China by the Silk Road in 629, crossing its deserts and mountains on his way to India.

cards.tx: Voyager. Scholar.
cards.fact: A Buddhist monk, he left China in 629 without the emperor's leave and was gone sixteen years, travelling to India and back. He came home with hundreds of Buddhist books, and the story of his journey grew into the tales of the Monkey King.
cards.art: Xuanzang, a Chinese Buddhist monk of twenty-seven, crossing the desert beyond the last watchtower of China alone in the year 629, by night: a thin young man with a shaved head, in patched grey and brown monk's robes with a cloth wound around his lower legs, walking beside a lean old reddish horse and resting one hand on its neck. His water skin hangs empty and flat from the saddle. He is looking up, lips parted, at a sky crowded with stars, and ahead on the sand lie the scattered white bones of a camel that mark the track. Far behind, a tiny signal fire burns on a mud-brick watchtower. Seen from a little ahead and below, from the knees up, his face in the upper half, right of centre. Tang China: no carrying frame hung with a lamp (that belongs to later paintings), no monkey or pig companions, no staff with rings. Keep the top left corner stars.

cards.tx: When you play a Relic, draw a card.
cards.fact: Chief engineer at a palace on the upper Tigris, he finished a book in 1206 that explains, with coloured drawings, how to build fifty machines. Among them are water clocks, pumps, fountains and a boat of mechanical musicians that played to guests at the king's parties.
cards.art: Al-Jazari, engineer at the Artuqid court, about 1200, finishing his elephant clock, drawn after the painting in his own book: a man of about sixty with a grey beard, in a long patterned robe and a turban, standing on a wooden step with his sleeve pushed back and his arm reaching into an open panel in the side of a brightly painted model elephant as tall as he is. On the elephant's back sits a small mahout figure and a square tower in which a little scribe sits; above the tower two dragons with open jaws curl around a post, and on the very top perches a bird. He is setting a bronze ball in place and watching the dragons. Tools, floats and lengths of cord lie on a bench. Composed with the flat bright colour of a medieval Arabic manuscript. Seen from the side, his face in the upper right. Twelfth-century Mesopotamia: no gears of steel, no clock face with hands. Keep the top left corner plain wall.

links.alkhwarizmi>fibonacci: Fibonacci learned the Indian numerals as a boy in North Africa, and his book draws on al-Khwarizmi and the Arab mathematicians who followed him.

cards.tx: Legacy of Al-Khwarizmi. On arrival, gain 1 Spark.
cards.fact: His book of 1202 showed the merchants of Europe how to reckon with the nine Indian figures and zero in place of Roman numerals. One of its puzzles, about a pair of breeding rabbits, gives the string of numbers that now bears his name.
cards.art: Leonardo of Pisa, called Fibonacci, about 1202, in a merchant's counting house in Pisa: a man of about thirty with dark hair cut straight across the brow and no beard, in a long belted tunic and a soft cap, standing at a sloping desk and writing a column of Indian numerals with a quill, quick and sure, while he holds up his left hand to stop an older merchant beside him who is still pushing counters about on a lined counting board. The older man stares at the finished sum. Sacks, a pair of scales and bolts of cloth fill the room, and through the open arch behind stands the cathedral's new bell tower, only three storeys built and already leaning. Seen from across the desk, from the waist up, Fibonacci's face in the upper right. Pisa about 1200: no printed books, no eyeglasses, the tower unfinished. Keep the top left corner plain stone wall.

links.press>gutenberg: Gutenberg built his press in Mainz about 1450 and printed his great Bible on it.

cards.tx: When you play a Relic, draw a card.
cards.fact: A goldsmith by training, he worked out how to cast metal letters by the thousand, all alike, in a small mould held in the hand. About 180 copies of his Bible were printed, and nearly fifty of them still exist.
cards.art: Johannes Gutenberg about 1450 in his workshop at Mainz, casting type: a man in his fifties in a plain dark gown with the sleeves rolled and a leather apron, a close cap on his head, standing by a small brick furnace. In his left hand he holds a little two-part mould of wood and iron that he has just snapped open, and a single bright new metal letter is dropping from it into his right palm; he peers at it closely. A ladle rests in the pot of molten metal, and on the bench are rows of finished letters, a file and a punch. Deep in the room behind, out of focus, stands the wooden press. Firelight on his face and hands. Seen from the bench, from the waist up, his face in the upper right. No portrait of him from life exists, so the face is an ordinary craftsman's: no long forked beard, no fur hat. Keep the top left corner dark beams.

links.astrolabe>dagama: On his way to India, Vasco da Gama stopped at a bay in southern Africa and measured the height of the Sun with an astrolabe to find how far south he had come.

cards.tx: Voyager: he can walk to any Place.
cards.fact: In 1498 he reached India by sailing around Africa, the first to link Europe and Asia by sea. On the way out he swung far into the open Atlantic to catch the winds and saw no land for about three months.
cards.art: Vasco da Gama in November 1497 on the beach of a bay in southern Africa, measuring the height of the Sun: a hard-faced Portuguese captain in his thirties with a full dark beard, in a padded doublet, hose and a flat cap, standing on the sand beside a large wooden astrolabe, a ring as wide as his arm is long, hung from a tripod of three poles. He stoops to sight along its pointer at the noon Sun while a pilot kneels to read the scale and a ship's boy writes the number down. Their boat is drawn up on the beach, and out in the bay ride his ships, small round-hulled vessels with red crosses on their square sails. Seen from the water's edge, from the knees up, his face in the upper right. Portugal in the 1490s: no telescope, no sextant, no tricorne hat. Keep the top left corner empty sky.
cards.check: One source says almost four months without sight of land (counted from Lisbon). The large wooden astrolabe on a tripod in the picture brief is from João de Barros and was not returned by the search.

cards.tx: Voyager. On arrival, gain 1 Spark.
cards.fact: He left Spain in 1519 with five ships and about 270 men to reach the Spice Islands by sailing west. He was killed in the Philippines, and three years after setting out a single ship came home with eighteen of the crew, the first to sail around the world.
cards.art: Ferdinand Magellan in March 1518 at Valladolid, persuading the young king of Spain: a short, thickset Portuguese of about thirty-eight with a heavy dark beard and a lame left leg, in a plain black doublet and cap, standing with a painted globe held in the crook of one arm and the forefinger of his other hand laid on the blank place at the foot of South America where he believes a strait must be. He looks straight up at the king, who is only a slim shape on a dais at the upper left edge, with a bishop bending to whisper to him. Beside Magellan a cosmographer unrolls a sea chart. A bare Castilian hall with a coffered ceiling. Seen from beside the dais, so that Magellan faces us from the waist up, his face and the globe in the upper right. Spain in 1518: no ruffs, no armour, the globe showing no Pacific islands. Keep the top left corner dark ceiling.
cards.check: The globe shown to the king in 1518 and his lame leg are in the picture brief only and were not returned by the search.

links.copernicus>kepler: Kepler's first book, printed in 1596, was a defence of Copernicus's Sun-centred system.

cards.tx: Legacy of Copernicus. Scholar.
cards.fact: Working for years through another astronomer's sightings of Mars, he found that the planets move in ovals, not circles, and travel faster when they are nearer the Sun. He also defended his own mother in court when she was accused of witchcraft, and she went free.
cards.art: Johannes Kepler in Prague about 1605, at the end of his long war with the planet Mars: a thin, slight man of thirty-three with a pointed dark beard, in a black doublet with a small white collar, bent very close over a huge sheet of paper, for his eyes were weak, drawing with a pen the long oval path of a planet with the Sun set to one side of its centre. His free hand presses flat a stack of pages filled edge to edge with columns of figures, and more discarded pages cover the floor. The candles have burned down and grey dawn shows at a small leaded window; a brass quadrant hangs on the wall. Seen from across the table, low, his face in the upper right. Prague in 1605: he has no telescope yet, no globe of the planets, no wig. Keep the top left corner plain wall.

cards.tx: Voyager: she can walk to any Place.
cards.fact: Living in Constantinople as the British ambassador's wife, she saw old women guard children against smallpox by scratching a little matter from a mild case into the skin. She had her own son treated in 1718, and back in London she pressed doubting doctors to try it.
cards.art: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu in Constantinople in March 1718, having her son protected against smallpox: an Englishwoman of twenty-eight with dark hair, her face lightly pitted by the smallpox she survived and her eyelashes gone, wearing the Turkish dress she adopted and was painted in, a long fitted coat of patterned silk over a fine shift and loose trousers, a small jewelled cap. She kneels on a carpet holding her five-year-old son firmly on her lap, his sleeve rolled to the shoulder, her eyes fixed on the work. An old Greek woman in a dark headscarf bends over the boy's arm with a needle in one hand and half a walnut shell in the other. A window shows domes and cypress trees. Seen from close, Lady Mary's face in the upper right. Ottoman Constantinople in 1718: no harem fantasy, no veils over faces, no doctor's instruments of a later age. Keep the top left corner plain wall.
cards.check: The year 1718 for her son's inoculation was not returned.

links.newton>duchatelet: Émilie du Châtelet put Newton's Principia into French, and hers is still the standard French translation.

cards.tx: Legacy of Isaac Newton. Scholar.
cards.fact: She translated Newton's great book from Latin into French and added pages of her own to explain its mathematics. She finished the work in 1749, only days before she died.
cards.art: Émilie du Châtelet in the summer of 1749, working through the night to finish her translation of Newton: a tall woman of forty-two with a long, lively face and dark hair loosely dressed and unpowdered, in a loose silk morning gown with the sleeves pushed back, seated at a table crowded with candles. A great Latin folio stands open on a reading stand before her; she writes fast on a sheet with her right hand while her left holds a pair of brass dividers stepped across a diagram of an orbit. Finished pages lie in a deep pile at her elbow, tied in bundles with ribbon, and a cold cup of coffee stands forgotten. A tall window is black with night. Seen from across the table, from the waist up, her face in the upper right. France in the 1740s: no towering wig, no court hoops, no chalkboard. Keep the top left corner dark panelled wall.

links.montagu>jenner: As a boy, Jenner was himself protected against smallpox by the method Lady Mary Wortley Montagu had brought to England.

cards.tx: Legacy of Lady Mary Wortley Montagu. Steadfast: he has +2 Might when he defends.
cards.fact: In 1796 he scratched matter from a milkmaid's cowpox sore into a boy's arm and showed that the boy could no longer catch smallpox. The word vaccine comes from vacca, the Latin for cow, and in 1980 smallpox became the first human disease to be wiped out everywhere.
cards.art: Edward Jenner in May 1796 in a Gloucestershire dairy, studying the hand of the milkmaid Sarah Nelmes: a country doctor about to turn forty-seven with a round, kindly face and his own brown hair tied back, in a blue coat, yellow waistcoat and riding boots, holding the young woman's right hand in both of his and turning it to the light from the door to look at the blisters of cowpox on her fingers. She stands in a cap and apron, patient and a little amused. Behind them a brown and white cow turns her head in the stall, and a milking stool and wooden pail stand in the straw. A leather pocket case lies open on a barrel. Seen from inside the shed, from the waist up, Jenner's face in the upper right. England in the 1790s: no syringe, no white coat, no powdered court wig. Keep the top left corner dark timber.

cards.tx: Voyager. Inspiring: your other Figures here get +1 Might.
cards.fact: For five years he explored South and Central America, measuring everything from the heat of the sea to the blue of the sky. In 1802 he climbed higher on the volcano Chimborazo than anyone on record had ever climbed.
cards.art: Alexander von Humboldt on 23 June 1802, high on the volcano Chimborazo in the Andes, at the crack in the ridge that stopped him: a slim man of thirty-two with windblown light brown hair, in an ordinary town coat, waistcoat and thin boots cut to pieces by the rock, his lips and gums bleeding from the thin air. He kneels on a knife-edge of black rock and snow, holding a long glass barometer upright in its case and reading it with fierce attention, while a companion steadies the foot of the instrument and a third man writes the figure with numb fingers. Cloud boils below them on both sides and the white dome of the summit hangs close above. Seen from just along the ridge, from the knees up, his face in the upper right. No ropes, ice axes or climbing clothes of later times, no fur. Keep the top left corner cloud.

cards.tx: When you play a Relic, draw a card.
cards.fact: She was twelve when she and her brother dug an ichthyosaur out of the sea cliffs near their home, and she went on to find the first complete plesiosaur. She sold fossils for a living, and the learned men who bought them seldom gave her the credit.
cards.art: Mary Anning in December 1823 on the shore below the dark cliffs of Lyme Regis, uncovering the first complete plesiosaur: a sturdy young woman of twenty-four with a weathered face, in a heavy wool cloak, a long plain dress with mud to the knees and a bonnet tied down with a scarf, kneeling on a ledge of grey shale just washed bare by a winter storm. With a small hammer and chisel she is freeing the long line of neck bones that runs across the ledge to a tiny skull, and she has stopped, hammer lifted, to look at how long the neck is. A basket of tools stands beside her and her small black and white dog sits watching. Grey sea, wet rock, a landslip of clay behind. Seen from the seaward side, her face in the upper right, the fossil running down to the lower left. England in the 1820s: no dinosaur shown alive, no magnifying lens, no trousers. Keep the top left corner cliff and sky.

links.rosetta>champollion: The Rosetta Stone, with its Greek text beside the Egyptian, gave Champollion the way in to reading hieroglyphs.

cards.tx: Scholar: you draw a card when he arrives.
cards.fact: As a schoolboy he taught himself one ancient language after another, among them Coptic, the last form of ancient Egyptian. In 1822 he worked out how to read hieroglyphs, which nobody had been able to read for some fourteen centuries.
cards.art: Jean-François Champollion at noon on 14 September 1822, in his attic study in Paris, at the instant he understands the hieroglyphs: a dark, curly-haired man of thirty-one with a full face, in shirtsleeves and an open waistcoat, half risen from his chair so suddenly that it is tipping over behind him. In one hand he grips a sheet of paper copied from a temple wall, on which a ring of picture signs is drawn in ink, a sun disc first among them; his other hand is flat on the table among dictionaries and sheets of the same signs set out in rows. His mouth is open in a shout. Sunlight from a small window falls across the papers. Seen from across the table, from the waist up, his face in the upper right. Paris in 1822: no pith helmet, no pyramids through the window, no mummy. Keep the top left corner sloping attic ceiling.

cards.tx: Inspiring: your other Figures here get +1 Might.
cards.fact: In a British army hospital in the Crimean War she fought for clean wards, fresh air and decent food, and far fewer soldiers died. She was also a gifted statistician, and drew a new kind of chart to show that dirt and disease were killing more men than battle.
cards.art: Florence Nightingale in the winter of 1854 on her night round of the army hospital at Scutari: a slender woman of thirty-four with a calm, firm face and brown hair parted in the middle under a small white cap, in a plain black wool dress with a white collar and a short dark cape. She carries the lamp she really used, a Turkish lantern of folded waxed cloth like a small concertina with a metal top and base and a candle inside, held low at her side so that its glow lights her face from below. She has stopped at one of the low beds that line an endless corridor and bends to lay two fingers on the wrist of a sleeping soldier. The rows of beds vanish into the dark behind her. Seen from the foot of the bed, from the waist up, her face in the upper right. No brass oil lamp with a spout, no nurse's apron with a red cross, no starched veil. Keep the top left corner darkness.

links.jenner>pasteur: Pasteur gave his own method the name vaccination, in honour of Jenner's work with cowpox.

cards.tx: Legacy of Edward Jenner. Steadfast: he has +2 Might when he defends.
cards.fact: He showed that germs spoil food and cause disease, and that gentle heat kills them, which is why milk is pasteurised. In 1885 his new vaccine saved a nine-year-old boy who had been badly bitten by a rabid dog.
cards.art: Louis Pasteur in July 1885 in his laboratory in Paris, on the day the boy Joseph Meister is first treated: a grey-bearded man of sixty-two with a grave, anxious face, in a dark coat and a small black skullcap, his left arm held a little stiffly at his side. He stands with his right hand resting on the shoulder of a nine-year-old boy in a short jacket, whose bandaged hands and leg show the dog bites, and he watches without blinking as a doctor in the background draws liquid into a small glass syringe. On the bench beside them stand glass flasks with long bent necks and a tall jar in which a strip of dried tissue hangs from a thread. Daylight from a high window. Seen from the bench, from the waist up, Pasteur's face in the upper right, the boy lower and to the left. France in the 1880s: no white coats, no microscope held to the eye, no electric light. Keep the top left corner plain wall.

links.verne>bly: Nellie Bly set out in 1889 to beat the eighty days of Jules Verne's novel, and stopped in France on the way to meet him.

cards.tx: Voyager. Swift: she can walk on the turn she arrives.
cards.fact: A newspaper reporter, she went around the world alone in 1889 and 1890 with one small bag, by steamer, train, rickshaw and donkey, in seventy-two days. Two years earlier she had pretended to be mad to get herself locked in an asylum for ten days, and wrote about the cruelty she found there.

She stands on the open rear platform of a railway carriage with one hand gripping the iron rail and the other holding up a small leather handbag, the only luggage she carried, laughing into the wind as the track streams away behind. On a prairie station platform slipping past, a crowd waves hats and handkerchiefs. Steam and snow. Seen from the trackside, from the knees up, her face in the upper right. He has stopped work; his pen hangs loose in his fingers and his head is turned to the tall window, where over the roofs of the old town a tram is drawing away down the street from a medieval clock tower with a great painted dial. On the table are stacks of messages in five-letter groups, pencils, and a cipher machine like a typewriter in an open wooden box, with three small wheels at the top. He holds his right hand open at shoulder height in greeting, and his sheathed short sword hangs untouched at his belt. She holds a purse in one hand and with the other points down to show the well-diggers where to go on, and a mason beside her is marking out the line of a wall with pegs and cord. Baskets of sand and yellow earth dug from the plot itself stand all around, and a first course of stone and brick is rising. Low houses of the young town and the green hills beyond. Around him rise the mosque's rows of columns carrying double arches striped in red brick and pale stone, and beyond them orange trees stand in a sunlit court. He sits on a low broad couch spread with a tiger skin and holds up between two fingers a large oblong sheet of dark grey paper money stamped with red seals, weighing it against a string of bronze coins that hangs from his other hand. A Chinese official kneels with a lacquer tray of more notes, and a Persian minister and a Mongol guard stand behind. Red lacquered pillars and a felt hanging. He looks down past his shoulder. Men lean out from the battlements above, paying out the ropes. Far below on the plain spread the tents and horse lines of an enormous army in the first light, and a small party of riders waits at the foot of the wall. He stands on the half-built causeway, a double row of timber stakes packed with stone and earth, holding a knotted measuring cord, and looks along its line to where it runs out across the water. Canoes heaped with rock are poled in on one side; on the calm lake behind lie floating gardens and the white temples of a far island city. Volcanoes with snow on the skyline. He sits on a floor cushion at a low table and holds two fingers to his own throat while he sounds a syllable aloud, his eyes narrowed with poor sight, and with his other hand he points to a sheet on which a young scholar has brushed a few plain shapes: a circle, a short bar, an angle. Three more scholars in blue robes and tall black hats lean in, one mouthing the same sound. Paper lanterns and a folding screen painted with mountains. She has pushed back her chair and leans forward with one hand flat on the tablecloth and the other raised, a forefinger marking her point, speaking straight across the table to a row of gentlemen in dark coats, one of whom has his mouth open to interrupt and another of whom has put down his knife to listen. A plain meal of boiled fish and vegetables, wine glasses, candles. A print hangs on the wall. Seen from the men's side of the table, so that she faces us from the waist up, her face in the upper right. London in the 1790s: no powdered wig, no wide court skirts, no bonnet. Keep the top left corner plain wall.

cards.fact: She became queen at eighteen and reigned for sixty-three years, while railways, telegraphs and steamships tied a quarter of the world's people into her empire. Her nine children married into so many royal families that she was called the grandmother of Europe.
cards.art: Victoria at six in the morning on 20 June 1837, a month after her eighteenth birthday, learning that she is queen: a very small young woman with a round face, large blue eyes and light brown hair hanging loose down her back, in a white dressing gown with a shawl over it and slippers, standing just inside the door of a sitting room at Kensington Palace. Before her two men in black have gone down on one knee, an old archbishop and a court official, and the official is lifting his face to tell her the news. She holds out her hand for them to kiss, pale but composed. Early light comes through tall windows; a candle still burns on a table. Seen from behind the kneeling men, so that she faces us from the waist up, her face in the upper right. England in 1837: no crown, no widow's cap, no black dress, no old queen. Keep the top left corner window curtain.
cards.check: The morning of her accession was confirmed from her own journal; the 63 years and nine children were not returned.

links.@seneca>stanton: Elizabeth Cady Stanton lived in Seneca Falls, helped call the convention of 1848 and wrote most of its declaration.

cards.fact: At a meeting she helped call in her own small town in 1848, she read out a declaration that all men and women are created equal, and asked for the vote. She worked for it for the rest of her life, and American women won it eighteen years after she died.
cards.art: Elizabeth Cady Stanton at thirty-two, on 16 July 1848, drafting the declaration for the convention at a friend's parlour table: a short, lively woman with dark curls gathered at each side of her face, in a striped silk day dress with a lace collar, seated at a small round mahogany tea table. She writes with a steel pen, and with her left hand she holds flat a printed copy of the American Declaration of Independence, running her finger under a line as she changes its words. An older Quaker woman in a plain grey dress and white cap sits beside her, reading the last sheet, and a third leans over the back of the chair. An ink bottle, a tea tray pushed aside, summer light through muslin curtains. Seen from across the little table, from the waist up, her face in the upper right. New York State in 1848: no sash, no placards, no white hair. Keep the top left corner wallpaper.

cards.tx: He has +2 Might while he is outnumbered here.
cards.fact: He lived for two years in a cabin he built himself beside Walden Pond, to find out how little a person needs. He once spent a night in jail for refusing to pay a tax to a government that allowed slavery, and wrote an essay about it that was read around the world.
cards.art: Henry David Thoreau at twenty-seven, in the spring of 1845, building his cabin in the woods by Walden Pond: a short, wiry man with a large nose, deep-set grey-blue eyes and rough brown hair, clean-shaven, in shirtsleeves, a waistcoat and patched trousers. He stands inside the bare frame of a tiny house, one room, and is fitting a rafter, holding it up with one arm and a borrowed axe in the other hand, his head tipped back to judge the line against the sky. Hewn pine timbers lie about, with a heap of second-hand boards and two old windows leaning against a tree. Through the pines the pond shines below. Seen from inside the frame, from the knees up, his face in the upper right. New England in 1845: no beard yet, no log cabin of round logs (it was a framed and boarded house), no rifle. Keep the top left corner pine branches.
cards.check: Not returned by the search. Walden, the night in jail in 1846 and the essay are standard, written from memory.

links.douglass>lincoln: Frederick Douglass went to the White House in 1863 to press Lincoln for fair treatment of Black soldiers, and Lincoln sent for him again the next year to ask his advice.

cards.tx: He has +1 Might for each of your other Figures here.
cards.fact: Born in a one-room log cabin, with less than a year of school in all, he taught himself law and became president as the United States broke in two. He held the Union together through four years of civil war and signed the order that began the end of slavery.
cards.art: Abraham Lincoln in the summer of 1862, in the telegraph office of the War Department, where he went to read the news from the armies and where he began to write the order of emancipation: a very tall, gaunt man of fifty-three with a deeply lined face, a dark beard without a moustache and untidy black hair, in a black frock coat with a grey wool shawl around his shoulders. He sits hunched at a borrowed desk by the window, his long legs folded under it, writing a line slowly on a sheet of foolscap and then gazing out at the street; his tall hat stands upside down on the desk with papers in it. Behind him two young operators bend over clicking brass telegraph keys. Seen from across the desk, from the waist up, his face in the upper right. Washington in 1862: no monument, no flag draped behind, no log cabin. Keep the top left corner window light and wall.

links.stanton>anthony: Susan B. Anthony met Elizabeth Cady Stanton in 1851, and the two worked side by side for women's rights for fifty years.

cards.fact: In 1872 she walked into a polling place in Rochester and voted for president, which the law did not allow a woman to do. She was arrested, tried and fined a hundred dollars, and she never paid a cent of it.
cards.art: Susan B. Anthony at fifty-two, on 18 November 1872, in the front parlour of her house in Rochester as a deputy marshal comes to arrest her for voting: a tall, spare woman with a firm mouth, her greying hair parted in the middle and drawn smoothly back into a knot, small wire spectacles, a black silk dress with a white lace collar and a red shawl over her shoulders. She stands facing him and holds out both wrists together, demanding to be handcuffed like any other prisoner, while the marshal, a young man in a tall hat and overcoat, shifts on the carpet, embarrassed, hat half raised. Her sister watches from the doorway. A horsehair sofa, a lamp, lace curtains. Seen from behind the marshal's shoulder, so that she faces us from the waist up, her face in the upper right. America in 1872: no banner, no sash, no crowd. Keep the top left corner wallpaper and picture rail.
cards.check: Her demand to be handcuffed is in the picture brief only and was not returned.

links.thoreau>gandhi: Gandhi read Thoreau's essay on civil disobedience in South Africa and printed parts of it in his own newspaper.
links.tolstoy>gandhi: Gandhi exchanged letters with Tolstoy in the last year of the old writer's life, and named his community in South Africa Tolstoy Farm.

cards.fact: He led India toward independence without weapons, by refusing to obey unjust laws and accepting the punishment. In 1930 he walked 240 miles to the sea with a growing crowd and picked up a handful of salt, breaking a law that taxed it.
cards.art: Mohandas Gandhi about 1930, aged sixty, at his daily spinning in the community where he lived in western India: a small, thin, brown man with a shaved head, large ears, round wire spectacles and a grey moustache, wearing only a short white homespun cloth wrapped at the waist and a white shawl over one shoulder. He sits cross-legged on the bare floor of an open verandah at a small wooden spinning wheel that folds flat into a box, turning the wheel with his right hand and drawing out a long fine thread of cotton with his left, raised high, his eyes on the thread. Beside him are a little pile of cotton slivers, a pocket watch on a string and a stack of letters held down by a stone. Whitewashed wall, a neem tree, morning light. Seen from the floor in front of him, from the waist up, his face in the upper right. No crowd, no flag, no walking staff in this picture. Keep the top left corner plain white wall.
cards.check: Accounts of the Salt March give 78 to 80 companions and 200 to 240 miles.

links.gandhi>king: Martin Luther King studied Gandhi's campaigns, and travelled to India in 1959 to meet people who had worked beside him.

cards.fact: A Baptist minister, he led marches, boycotts and sit-ins against laws that kept Black and white Americans apart, and was jailed for it about thirty times. In 1963 he told a quarter of a million people in Washington of his dream that children would be judged by their character, not their colour.
cards.art: Martin Luther King Jr. at twenty-seven, on the night of 30 January 1956 in Montgomery, Alabama, on the porch of his own house an hour after it was bombed: a compact young Black man with a round, serious face and a thin moustache, in a dark overcoat over a suit and tie, hatless, standing at the top of the porch steps with one hand raised, palm out, speaking quietly. The front window behind him is blown in and the porch boards are splintered. Below him in the dark yard a crowd of his neighbours has gathered, angry, some with sticks and bottles, and as he speaks the nearest of them are lowering what they hold. Two white policemen stand uneasily at the edge of the lamplight. Seen from in the crowd, looking up, King from the knees up, his face in the upper right. Alabama in 1956: no podium, no microphones, no monument. Keep the top left corner night sky and porch roof.

links.gandhi>mandela: The campaign of peaceful law-breaking that Mandela helped lead in 1952 followed the method Gandhi had first tried in South Africa.

cards.tx: Legacy of Gandhi. Steadfast: he has +2 Might when he defends.
cards.fact: He spent twenty-seven years in prison for fighting laws that set South Africans apart by the colour of their skin. Four years after he walked free he was elected president, and he asked the country to forgive and not to take revenge.
cards.art: Nelson Mandela about 1965, aged forty-seven, a prisoner in the lime quarry on Robben Island: a tall, broad-shouldered man with close-cropped hair, a strong jaw and a steady look, in the prison dress given to Black prisoners there, a khaki shirt, short trousers and sandals without socks. He stands in the white glare of the quarry floor with a pick resting head-down on the ground under his folded hands, and has turned to speak to a half circle of other prisoners who sit on blocks of lime in the mouth of a shallow cave cut in the quarry face, one of them drawing in the dust with a finger as if at a lesson. A warder with a rifle stands far off on the rim. Everything is bleached white and the men squint against it. Seen from the cave mouth, Mandela from the knees up, his face in the upper right. No bars, no raised fist, no grey-haired elder statesman. Keep the top left corner pale quarry wall.
cards.check: The 27 years, the release in 1990, the election of 1994 and the lime quarry were confirmed. The search did not return that the 1952 campaign followed Gandhi's method.

cards.tx: She has +2 Might while you have more Figures here than the other player.
cards.fact: A queen of China's Shang dynasty, she led armies of up to thirteen thousand soldiers, as questions scratched on oracle bones record. Her tomb was found untouched in 1976, with more than a hundred bronze weapons in it, among them four great battle-axes.
cards.art: Fu Hao, queen and general of Shang dynasty China, about 1200 BC, before her army on the morning of a campaign: a strong woman in her thirties with a commanding face, her black hair coiled high and held with a row of long carved bone pins, in a robe of patterned silk with a wide sash and a collar of jade beads. She stands on a rammed-earth platform holding upright before her, in both hands, a huge bronze axe of command, its broad blade cast with two tigers facing a human head between them, green-gold in the early light. Below the platform her soldiers stand in ranks with bronze dagger-axes on long shafts and painted leather shields, and a few two-horse chariots wait at the wings. A bronze cauldron on three legs smokes beside her. Seen from the foot of the platform, from the knees up, her face in the upper right. Bronze Age China: no iron, no crossbows, no riders on horseback, no later dragon robes. Keep the top left corner pale dawn sky.
cards.check: The tomb, the 130 weapons and the four axes were confirmed; the 13,000 soldiers were not returned.

links.cyrus>tomyris: The Greek historian Herodotus says that Cyrus the Great died fighting the army of Queen Tomyris.

cards.fact: Queen of the Massagetae, horse people of the plains east of the Caspian Sea, she refused to marry Cyrus the Great and hand him her country. The Greek historian Herodotus says her army then beat his in the fiercest battle he had ever heard of.
cards.art: Tomyris, queen of the Massagetae, about 530 BC, on the bank of the great river that bounds her country, giving her answer to the envoy of the king of Persia: a woman in her forties with a weathered, proud face and long dark braids, in the dress of the steppe riders as their own goldwork shows it, a belted tunic sewn with small gold plaques, trousers tucked into soft boots, and a tall pointed felt headdress ornamented with gold. A bow in its combined case and quiver hangs at her left hip and a short sword at her right. She stands on foot holding her horse by the rein and points with her whole arm back across the river, sending the envoy away; he bows in a long Persian robe, with an unrolled offer in his hands. On the far bank men are lashing boats together into a bridge. Seen from beside the envoy, so that she faces us from the knees up, her face in the upper right. No severed head, no bloodshed, no Greek armour. Keep the top left corner wide sky.
cards.check: Other ancient writers tell the death of Cyrus differently; the card gives it as Herodotus's account.

cards.fact: He won the wrestling at six Olympic Games, over more than twenty years. The Greeks told how he trained by carrying a calf on his shoulders every day until it had grown into a bull.
cards.art: Milo of Croton as a young man about 535 BC, in the story the Greeks told of his training: a huge, thick-necked wrestler of about twenty with short curly hair and a boxer's flattened ears, in a short belted tunic, walking up a stony hill path outside his city with a half-grown bull calf laid across his shoulders behind his neck, gripping its fore and hind legs in his two fists in front of his chest. His head is bent forward under the weight, his jaw is set, and the calf looks out mildly over his shoulder. Small boys run alongside, counting his steps. Olive trees, a white temple and the sea far below. The picture is the legend, so the calf is already almost too big to carry. Seen from ahead of him on the path, from the knees up, his face in the upper half, right of centre. Greek Italy in the sixth century BC: no gladiator gear, no lion skin, no club. Keep the top left corner sky and olive leaves.

links.caesar>vercingetorix: Vercingetorix led the tribes of Gaul against Julius Caesar, and gave himself up to him at Alesia in 52 BC.

cards.fact: At about thirty he joined the quarrelling tribes of Gaul into one army against Julius Caesar and beat him at Gergovia. Trapped at last in the hill town of Alesia, he rode out and gave himself up to spare his starving people.
cards.art: Vercingetorix in the spring of 52 BC on the rampart of the hill fort of Gergovia, as the Roman attack on it fails: a tall young chieftain of about thirty with long fair hair swept back and a heavy moustache, no beard, in a shirt of iron mail over a checked wool tunic and trousers, a twisted gold ring around his neck and a cloak pinned at the shoulder. He stands on top of a wall of timber, stone and earth with a long iron sword pointing down the slope and his head thrown back, shouting to the chiefs of other tribes who crowd the rampart beside him under their own boar standards, men who were enemies a month ago. Below, Roman soldiers are falling back down the steep hillside in disorder. Seen from on the rampart, from the knees up, his face in the upper right. Gaul in the first century BC: no winged or horned helmet, no bare-chested barbarian, no plaid kilt. Keep the top left corner sky and smoke.

cards.tx: Raider: she has +2 Might when she attacks on the other player's side.
cards.fact: Queen of Kush, on the Nile south of Egypt, she fought the Romans for about five years after they took Egypt. The peace she won fixed the border and freed her kingdom from the tax Rome had demanded.
cards.art: Amanirenas, the Kandake of Kush, about 24 BC at her capital Meroë, drawn after the carved reliefs of the queens of Kush: a powerfully built woman of middle age, blind in one eye as a Greek writer of her time recorded, with the lid of that eye closed, in a long fringed robe with a tasselled sash over one shoulder, a close-fitting cap with a rearing cobra at the brow, heavy bead collars and wide gold bracelets, a broad-bladed spear in her left hand. She stands at the foot of a temple stair and points down with her right hand as two soldiers lower a bronze head, the head of a statue of a young Roman with inlaid staring eyes, into a pit dug under the lowest step, where every foot will tread on it. Small steep-sided pyramids stand on the ridge behind. Seen from across the pit, from the knees up, her face in the upper right. Kush, not Egypt: no striped pharaoh's headcloth, no Cleopatra costume, no leopard-skin fantasy. Keep the top left corner temple wall.
cards.check: Her one blind eye (Strabo) is in the picture brief only and was not returned.

links.augustus>arminius: Arminius destroyed three of Augustus's legions, and the Roman writer Suetonius says the old emperor cried out for his general to give them back.

cards.fact: A chief's son of the Cherusci, he had served as an officer with the Roman army and knew how it fought. In AD 9 he drew three legions into forest and bog in the rain and destroyed them, and Rome gave up its plan to rule the lands beyond the Rhine.
cards.art: Arminius in September of AD 9, aged about twenty-six, at the edge of the forest on the morning he turns on Rome: a tall young German noble with reddish-fair hair combed to one side and tied in a knot above his temple, a short beard, and the mail shirt and long cavalry sword of a Roman officer of the allied horse, which he has been. He has reined in out of sight of the marching column, dismounted, and is pulling the red Roman officer's cloak from his shoulders with one hand to let it fall in the mud, while with the other he grips the forearm of an older chief in a wool cloak and trousers who has stepped from the trees. Behind the chief the wood is full of half-seen warriors with spears and long narrow shields. Rain, dripping oaks, wet ferns. Seen from between the trees, from the knees up, his face in the upper right. No winged or horned helmets, no fur loincloths, no battle yet. Keep the top left corner dark leaves.
cards.check: His Roman service, the three legions and AD 9 were confirmed. The search did not return the words Suetonius gives Augustus (Suetonius, Augustus 23).

cards.fact: Trưng Trắc and her sister Trưng Nhị raised northern Vietnam against its Chinese rulers in AD 40 and took sixty-five towns. They ruled as queens for about three years, and Vietnam still honours them every year.
cards.art: The two Trưng sisters, Trắc and Nhị, in the spring of AD 40 at the mouth of the Hát River in northern Vietnam, calling their people to rise: two young noblewomen of the Lạc people, the elder a little taller, with their hair wound up in cloth, in wrapped skirts and short jackets with broad woven belts, each with a short bronze sword at her side. They stand on a river bluff on either side of a great bronze drum that reaches to their waists, its flat top cast with a many-pointed star and rings of flying birds; the elder sister is bringing a wooden mallet down on the star with both hands, and the younger holds a spear upright and looks out over the water. Below them long war canoes crowded with men and women are pulling in to the bank from every side. Seen from just below the bluff, both sisters from the knees up, their faces in the upper half, right of centre. Vietnam two thousand years ago: no elephants in this picture, no silk court robes of later dynasties, no conical hats. Keep the top left corner river mist.

cards.fact: Queen of the desert trading city of Palmyra, she took Egypt and much of the Roman East in two years and ruled it in her young son's name. Scholars were welcome at her court, and she was said to speak several languages.
cards.art: Zenobia, queen of Palmyra, about AD 270, sending her army out to Egypt along the city's great colonnaded street: a dark-eyed woman of about thirty with a strong, intent face, dressed as the carved portraits of Palmyra's noblewomen show them, in a long embroidered tunic with a cloak pinned at the left shoulder by a large brooch, a jewelled band across her forehead under a wound headcloth, heavy earrings and many bracelets. She stands on the steps at the foot of a four-pillared monument with a soldier's helmet held in the crook of her arm and her other hand lifted in salute. Past her down the street, between two endless rows of tall honey-coloured columns, rides her heavy cavalry, men and horses alike covered in scale armour, with long lances. Seen from the roadway, from the knees up, her face in the upper right. Roman Syria: no chains, no Roman triumph, no belly-dancer costume, no veil across the face. Keep the top left corner column tops and sky.

cards.fact: Born Temüjin, he was left fatherless and hunted as a boy. In 1206 he joined the warring peoples of the steppe into one nation, and his riders went on to build the largest land empire in history, tied together by relays of mounted messengers.
cards.art: Temüjin in the spring of 1206 by the Onon River in Mongolia, at the great gathering where he is named Genghis Khan: a tall, strongly built man in his forties with a broad forehead, a long beard and watchful, cat-like eyes, as a Persian writer who spoke to those who had seen him described him, in a plain belted robe of blue wool that crosses over the chest, felt boots and a fur-edged cap, his hair in a braid behind each ear. He stands on a spread of white felt before a tall pole from which hang nine white horse tails, the standard of the new nation, and looks out over our heads. In front of him, at the bottom of the picture, the chiefs of the steppe peoples have taken off their caps and hung their belts around their necks, and are kneeling. Round felt tents and horse herds stretch to the hills. Seen from among the chiefs, from the knees up, his face in the upper right. cards.art: Richard, king of England, in June 1192 on a hilltop in Judea, within sight of Jerusalem and deciding to turn back: a very tall man of thirty-four with red-gold hair and a short beard, in a long shirt of mail with the mail hood pushed back on his shoulders, a plain linen surcoat over it and a sword belt, dusty and sunburned. He stands with his long kite-shaped shield lifted in his left hand so that its rim hides the far skyline from his own eyes, his head turned aside behind it, as an old story says he did, refusing to look at the city he could not take. He stands at the water's edge with a long narrow wooden shield on his left arm and a heavy single-edged sword that widens toward its tip held low in his right hand, perfectly still. Behind him his warriors are drawn up in three bodies with bamboo spears whose points are hardened in fire. Far out, beyond a reef that their boats cannot cross, men in steel helmets are climbing down into waist-deep water. Seen from the shallows, from the knees up, his face in the upper right. The Visayas in 1521: no feather headdress, no carved masks, no grass skirt. Keep the top left corner dawn sky and palm fronds.

cards.fact: A Mapuche boy captured by the Spanish, he served as groom to their governor and learned how horses and soldiers were used in battle. He escaped, taught his own people what he had seen, and at about nineteen beat the governor's army at Tucapel.
cards.art: Lautaro in 1553, aged about nineteen, back among his own Mapuche people in the south of Chile and teaching them the horse: a slim, quick young man with long black hair held by a woven band across his forehead, in a dark wool poncho with a pale stepped pattern over a wrapped lower garment, barefoot. He stands in a forest clearing holding a captured Spanish horse close by the bridle with one hand, calming it, and with the other he lifts an older warrior's hand and lays it flat on the animal's neck. The older man, who carries a long cane lance and a stone-headed club, leans away, wary. A ring of other warriors watches, and a Spanish saddle lies on the grass. Tall trees with branches like green ropes of scales stand around the clearing, with a snow-capped volcano above them. Seen from the edge of the ring, from the knees up, Lautaro's face in the upper right. Southern Chile in 1553: no feather war bonnet, no tipi, no Aztec or Inca dress. Keep the top left corner dark branches.

cards.fact: He fought his first duel at thirteen and, by his own count, won more than sixty without a defeat. Late in life he was also a painter, and in a cave he wrote down his way of the sword as The Book of Five Rings.
cards.art: Miyamoto Musashi in April 1612, aged about twenty-eight, on his way to the most famous duel of his life, as the old accounts tell it: a big, rough-looking swordsman with unshaven cheeks and long uncombed hair tied back with a strip of cloth, in a plain dark kimono with the sleeves tied up by a cord across his back. He sits in the bow of a small fishing boat rowed by one old boatman, shaving the blade of a spare oar into a long wooden sword with his short sword, curls of wood falling into the water, his eyes not on his hands but on the shore ahead. On a small flat island across the strait a tiny figure waits on the beach with a very long sword, and banners flutter behind him. Low morning sun in the rower's eyes. cards.art: Zumbi, leader of Palmares, about 1690, on the wooden wall of its hilltop capital in the forest of north-east Brazil: a strong Black man in his mid thirties with a short beard and a grave, alert face, in a loose cotton shirt, knee breeches and a cloth sash, a long iron-headed lance in his hand and a knife in his belt. Along the wall men and women are passing up bows, baskets of stones and a few muskets, and behind them lie thatched houses, a forge and fields of maize.
