cards.fact: He became king of the Maya city of Palenque at twelve and ruled for sixty-eight years, one of the longest reigns in history. In 1952 his tomb was found deep inside a pyramid, his face covered with a mask of jade.
cards.art: Pakal of Palenque on the day in the year 615 when he becomes king at twelve years old, drawn after the carved stone panel in his own palace that shows the scene: a slim boy with the long sloping forehead and high-bridged nose the Maya admired, his hair cut in steps and tied up in a plume, wearing a short kilt, a wide collar and wristbands of green jade beads. He sits cross-legged on a low throne carved as a jaguar with a head at each end, turned toward his mother, who kneels before him in a net-patterned dress and cape and lifts up to him in both hands a tall crown made of small plates of jade and shell. He reaches for it gravely with one hand. Behind them are the white plastered walls of a palace room painted with red bands, and through a doorway the roof combs of temples stand above the forest in mist. Seen from the side, Pakal from the waist up, his face in the upper right. The Maya of the seventh century: no Aztec sun stone, no feather war bonnet, no sacrifice. Keep the top left corner plain plaster wall.

cards.tx: Scholar: you draw a card when she arrives.
cards.fact: An abbess on the Rhine, she wrote down the visions she had seen since childhood, along with books about medicine and plants. More of her music survives than of any other composer of her time, some seventy songs with their words and their tunes.
cards.art: Hildegard of Bingen about 1150, aged fifty-two, receiving a vision and writing it down, drawn after the picture at the front of her own book: a woman with a pale, strong face lifted upward and wide grey eyes, in the black habit and veil of a Benedictine nun, seated on a wooden chair in a small arched cell. From a square opening in the roof above her five long tongues of red and gold flame reach down and touch her forehead, and she, without looking at her hands, is writing with a pointed stylus on a pair of hinged wax tablets held on her knee. At the right edge a tonsured monk, her secretary, has put his head through a little window in the cell wall and stares up at the flames, a sheet of parchment forgotten in his hand. Composed with the flat colour and gold ground of a twelfth-century manuscript painting. Seen from inside the cell, from the waist up, her face in the upper half, right of centre. No halo, no harp, no witch's herbs. Keep the top left corner plain painted arch.

cards.tx: He can't be moved. He has +1 Might for each round he stays, up to +2.
cards.fact: King of Ethiopia, he is remembered for eleven churches at his capital that were not built up from the ground but carved down into it, each cut from the solid rock. Pilgrims still come to pray in them, and the town now bears his name.
cards.art: Lalibela, king of Ethiopia, about the year 1200, at the rim of the pit in which one of his churches is being carved downward out of the living rock: a lean, dark, bearded man of middle age with a calm, absorbed face, in long white cotton robes with a coloured border, a white cloth wound around his head beneath a plain gold band, holding a tall staff topped with a cross. He stands at the very edge of a deep square trench cut in a hillside of red-brown stone and looks down into it. Below him, at the bottom of the picture, the flat roof of the church is already finished, a great cross within a cross carved in the rock, level with the ground, and far down around its walls tiny masons on ladders are hollowing out windows and doors with iron picks and carrying away baskets of chips. Priests in white stand behind the king with a drum and a book. Seen from across the trench, the king from the knees up, his face in the upper right. No angels shown, no European crown, no built stonework of blocks. Keep the top left corner dry hillside and sky.
cards.check: Tradition gives all eleven churches to his reign; some scholars think the work ran longer.

links.suleiman>sinan: Sinan was Suleiman's chief architect, and built for him the great mosque in Istanbul that bears the sultan's name.

cards.fact: He began as a soldier who built bridges for the Ottoman army, and was about fifty when he was made the sultan's chief architect. In the next fifty years he designed more than three hundred buildings, among them mosques whose wide domes seem to float on light.
cards.art: Sinan, chief architect of the Ottoman sultans, about 1555, aged about sixty-five, on the building site of the great mosque he is raising for Sultan Suleiman: a tall, straight-backed old man with a long white beard and keen eyes, in a plain long robe with a sash and a large white turban, standing on the unpaved floor of an enormous unfinished hall. In his left arm he carries a wooden model of the mosque, the size of a small chest, with its central dome and half domes, and with his right hand he points from the model up to the real dome high overhead, where a ring of forty arched windows is still open to the sky and timber centring fills the curve. Master masons with squares and plumb lines listen to him. Shafts of dusty daylight slant down past four huge piers. Seen from the floor in front of him, from the knees up, his face in the upper right. The sixteenth century: no finished tiles or carpets, no later baroque ornament, no fez. Keep the top left corner shadowed pier.
cards.check: His three hundred buildings and his start as a builder of army bridges were not returned.

links.elizabeth>grace: Grace O'Malley sailed to England in 1593 and put her case to Queen Elizabeth face to face.

cards.cap: Clew Bay, Ireland, c. 1530 to c. 1603
cards.tx: Voyager. Raider: she has +2 Might when she attacks on the other player's side.
cards.fact: Chieftain of a seafaring clan on the west coast of Ireland, she commanded her own fleet of galleys for decades, and the English called her a pirate. At about sixty-three she sailed to London and argued her case before Queen Elizabeth, who granted most of what she asked.
cards.art: Grace O'Malley, Gráinne Ní Mháille, about 1577, at her tower house on the shore of Clew Bay in the west of Ireland, sending her galleys to sea: a tall, weathered woman in her late forties with grey-streaked dark hair blowing loose and a hard, humorous face, in the dress of a Gaelic noblewoman, a full-sleeved linen tunic dyed yellow under a heavy fringed wool mantle fastened at the breast, a long knife at her belt. She stands at the head of the sea steps under a plain square stone tower, one hand on the wet rock, the other pointing out to the mouth of the bay, calling an order down to the nearer of two long, low ships with a single mast and a row of oars on each side, whose crews are pushing off. A mooring rope runs from the ship up through a slit window of the tower above her. Islands, rain cloud and a gap of bright sea. Seen from the water below the steps, from the knees up, her face in the upper right. Sixteenth-century Ireland: no eyepatch, no three-cornered hat, no skull flag, no cannon broadside. Keep the top left corner tower wall and cloud.
cards.check: Accounts differ on whether she and the queen spoke in Latin or English; the card does not say.

cards.tx: On arrival, gain 2 Spark.
cards.fact: When his wife Mumtaz Mahal died in 1631, the emperor of India set some twenty thousand workers to build her a tomb of white marble, the Taj Mahal. He spent his last eight years a prisoner of his own son, in a fort from which he could see it across the river.
cards.art: Shah Jahan about 1665, in his seventies, a prisoner in the fort at Agra, looking across the river at the tomb he built for his wife: a thin, upright old man with a long white beard and a fine, sad face, in a plain white muslin coat tied at the side and a small turban with a single pearl, seated on a cushion in an eight-sided marble pavilion whose walls are inlaid with flowers of coloured stone. He sits turned away from the room, one hand on the carved marble screen of the balcony, gazing out. Beyond the screen the wide river bends away in the haze of early morning, and on its far bank, small and pale and perfect, stand the white dome and four slim towers of the Taj Mahal. His eldest daughter sits behind him with a book. Seen from inside the pavilion, a little to one side, the emperor from the waist up, his face in profile in the upper right, the tomb in the distance at the centre left. Mughal India: no jewelled throne, no courtiers, no sword. Keep the top left corner inlaid marble wall.

links.wollstonecraft>shelley: Mary Shelley was Mary Wollstonecraft's daughter. Her mother died days after she was born, and she grew up reading her books.

cards.tx: Legacy of Mary Wollstonecraft. Scholar.
cards.fact: Kept indoors by storms at a house on Lake Geneva in the cold summer of 1816, she and her friends agreed that each would write a ghost story. She was eighteen, and hers became Frankenstein, the tale of a student who builds a living man and runs from what he has made.
cards.art: Mary Godwin, soon to be Mary Shelley, in June 1816, aged eighteen, on the stormy night at a villa above Lake Geneva when the idea of Frankenstein comes to her: a slight, fair girl with a high clear forehead, hazel eyes and light brown hair parted in the middle, in a plain high-waisted dress with a shawl. She stands alone at a tall window with one hand pressed flat to the glass and a candle in the other, and she has gone rigid, staring not at the lake but at something in her own mind; a fork of lightning over the black water and the far mountains lights her face white. Behind her in the room three young men talk by the fire, careless shapes in firelight with books and wine glasses, and none of them has noticed her. Rain on the panes. Seen from outside the window looking in, Mary from the waist up, her face in the upper right. 1816: no monster shown anywhere, no laboratory, no bolts, no castle. Keep the top left corner dark window frame and rain.

cards.tx: At the end of a round, if you hold his Place, draw a card.
cards.fact: A poor shoemaker's son, he left home alone at fourteen to seek his fortune in Copenhagen. He wrote more than 150 fairy tales, among them The Little Mermaid, The Ugly Duckling and The Emperor's New Clothes, and he could cut whole scenes out of folded paper while he told them.
cards.art: Hans Christian Andersen about 1850, aged forty-five, telling a story to the children of a Danish country house and cutting it out of paper as he goes: a very tall, thin, awkward man with a long nose, deep-set small eyes and a kind, mobile face, in a black frock coat with a high collar and a loose silk tie, perched on a chair too low for him with his knees up. In his big hands are a pair of enormous paper scissors and a folded sheet of white paper, from which he is just drawing apart, like a concertina, a long chain of joined figures: a row of dancers, a swan at each end, a little man in a tall hat. Four children press around his knees, one already holding an earlier cutting up to the window so that the daylight shines through it. A tiled stove, a rag rug. Seen from behind the smallest child, Andersen from the waist up, his face in the upper right. Denmark about 1850: no mermaid or duckling drawn in the room, no wizard's robe. Keep the top left corner plain wall.

cards.tx: On arrival, the strongest enemy Figure here misses its next turn.
cards.fact: He wrote poems and tales of dread, among them The Raven, and in 1841 he invented the detective story, with a hero who solves a murder by reasoning alone. He was found dying in Baltimore at forty, and nobody has ever explained what had happened to him.
cards.art: Edgar Allan Poe in the winter of 1846, aged thirty-seven, writing by night in his small cottage outside New York: a slight man with a very broad pale forehead, dark tumbled hair, a dark moustache and large, shadowed grey eyes, in a worn black coat buttoned to the neck against the cold. He sits at a bare table writing with a steel pen on a long narrow strip of paper made of sheets pasted end to end, which trails off the table and curls on the floor. A large tortoiseshell cat sits upright on his shoulder, as she really did, watching the pen. One candle; its light throws his shadow and the cat's, joined into a single strange tall shape, up the whitewashed wall behind him. A cold hearth and a few books on a hanging shelf. Seen from across the table, from the waist up, his face in the upper right. No raven, no skull, no bottle. Keep the top left corner bare wall above the shadow.
cards.check: The cat on his shoulder and the strips of pasted paper are in the picture brief only and were not returned.

links.poe>verne: Jules Verne admired Edgar Allan Poe's tales, and wrote a sequel to Poe's story of a voyage toward the South Pole.

cards.tx: Legacy of Edgar Allan Poe. Voyager: he can walk to any Place.
cards.fact: Before a submarine had crossed an ocean or anyone had left the ground in an aeroplane, he sent his heroes under the sea, around the Moon and around the world in eighty days, working out each journey with the science and the timetables of his day. He is one of the most translated authors there has ever been.
cards.art: Jules Verne about 1870, aged forty-two, writing in the tiny cabin of his own sailing boat on the coast of northern France, where he wrote much of his tale of a voyage under the sea: a broad-shouldered man with curly brown hair, a full beard and lively pale eyes, in a seaman's knitted jersey and a pea jacket, sitting wedged on a narrow bunk at a fold-down table that slopes with the boat. He writes in pencil in a thick notebook, steadying an inkwell with his elbow, and has looked up at the round brass-rimmed window beside his head, against which a green wave has just broken, so that for a moment the glass is full of water and light, as if the boat were under the sea. A sea chart, a lamp swinging on its hook, a row of scientific journals behind a rail. Seen from the cabin door, from the waist up, his face in the upper right. France about 1870: no submarine, no diving helmet, no balloon. Keep the top left corner dark deck beams.
cards.check: That he is among the most translated authors was not returned.

links.sittingbull>oakley: Sitting Bull saw Annie Oakley shoot in 1884, adopted her as a daughter, and gave her a name that means Little Sure Shot.

cards.tx: She has +2 Might when she attacks a stronger Figure.
cards.fact: She learned to shoot as a child to feed her family, and at fifteen she out-shot a travelling marksman, whom she later married. In Buffalo Bill's show she could hit the thin edge of a playing card at thirty paces.
cards.art: Annie Oakley about 1888, aged twenty-eight, in the arena of the Wild West show, making her most famous shot: a very small, neat woman with long dark hair down her back and a calm, intent face, in the costume she sewed herself, a calf-length skirt and a fitted jacket with a line of fringe, leggings, and a wide-brimmed hat pinned up at one side with a star, a row of shooting medals on her chest. She stands with her back to her target, a rifle laid over her right shoulder pointing behind her, and aims by looking into a small hand mirror that she holds up in her left hand; in the mirror we can just see the tiny reflection of a man far across the arena holding out a playing card edge-on. Her face is all concentration, one eye closed. Canvas tents, a grandstand full of hats. Seen from in front of her, from the waist up, her face in the upper right. No feathers, no short skirt, no two pistols twirling. Correct anatomy, two hands. Keep the top left corner tent canvas and sky.
cards.check: The playing card and the mirror shot were not returned. Sitting Bull's adoption of her was informal.

cards.tx: Swift. He can't be clashed.
cards.fact: Born Erik Weisz in Budapest, he could slip out of handcuffs, chains, jail cells and a locked tank of water in which he hung upside down. He also spent years exposing fake mediums who claimed to speak with the dead.
cards.art: Harry Houdini about 1916, aged forty-two, hanging head down in a straitjacket high above a city street: a short, very muscular man with curly dark hair standing out from his head and a face clenched with effort, his ankles bound in a padded harness to a rope that runs up to a beam jutting from the top of a tall newspaper building. He is strapped into a canvas straitjacket with leather buckles, his arms crossed and pinned, and he is doubled up at the waist, twisting, with one shoulder already worked half free. He fills the upper part of the picture, upside down, and far beneath him the whole street from wall to wall is a sea of upturned faces and straw hats, with stopped trams and people leaning from every window. Seen from a window level with him, his whole figure in the upper half, his face right of centre and the right way round enough to read. No chains, no water tank, no top hat or wand. Correct anatomy. Keep the top left corner sky and the edge of the building.

cards.tx: Voyager: she can walk to any Place.
cards.fact: In 1932 she became the first woman to fly alone across the Atlantic, landing in a farmer's field in Northern Ireland after nearly fifteen hours in the air. Five years later she vanished over the Pacific on a flight around the world, and no trace of her aeroplane has been confirmed.
cards.art: Amelia Earhart on 21 May 1932, aged thirty-four, minutes after landing alone from across the Atlantic in a cow pasture in the north of Ireland: a tall, slim woman with a freckled, wind-burned face, grey eyes and short tousled fair hair, in a leather flying jacket over a checked shirt, riding breeches and laced boots, a silk scarf at her neck. She is climbing out through the hatch in the roof of a bright red single-engined aeroplane with a high wing and a round nose, one leg over the edge, pulling off her leather helmet with one hand and laughing down, tired out, at a farm labourer in a flat cap who has run up and is staring at her with a hay fork still in his hand. Cows stand off at a distance. Wet green hills, stone walls, low cloud. Seen from the grass beside the labourer, Earhart from the knees up, her face in the upper right. No goggles over her eyes, no second person in the aeroplane, no ocean liner. Keep the top left corner cloud.
cards.check: The landing was at Culmore, near Derry.

links.hypatia>astrolabe: Hypatia's father Theon wrote a book on the astrolabe that later writers built on, and one of her students thanked her for teaching him how to make one.

cards.cap: Alexandria and Baghdad, from the 4th century
cards.tx: Your Figures can walk two steps.
cards.fact: With one brass disc a traveller could tell the time by the Sun or a star, find the direction of Mecca and measure the height of a tower. An astronomer of the tenth century described about a thousand uses for it.
cards.art: A brass astrolabe of the Islamic world, about the tenth century, hanging from a hand by the ring at its top against a clear night sky: a flat round instrument a little wider than the hand that holds it, its face an openwork plate of curling pointers, each one marking a star, laid over a disc engraved with fine arcs and circles, with a straight sighting bar pinned across the back. It turns slightly on its ring and catches lamplight. Behind it, out of focus, are the flat roofs and one dome of a city and a field of real stars that the pointers echo. Only the hand and wrist of the holder are in the picture, in a plain wide sleeve. Historically accurate: no glass, no magnetic needle, no numbers or letters that can be read. The instrument is in the upper half, right of centre. Keep the top left corner dark sky.
cards.check: The search corrected the first draft: Theon's book was not the earliest on the astrolabe.

links.cailun>paper: Cai Lun showed the Han court in 105 how to make good paper from bark, hemp, rags and old nets.

cards.tx: Draw one more card each turn.
cards.fact: For centuries only China knew how to make it. Paper reached Samarkand in the 700s and Baghdad before the year 800, and Spain about two hundred years after that, and wherever it arrived, books became cheaper.
cards.art: Newly made sheets of paper drying in the sun in a Chinese papermaker's yard of about the second century: a long whitewashed wall with a dozen pale, slightly rough-edged sheets pressed flat against it, the nearest one beginning to curl away at one corner in the breeze, its fibres catching the light. In front of the wall stand a wooden vat of grey pulp with a cloth-covered frame resting across it, a stone mortar, and a basket of bark strips, rags and a tangle of old fishing net. A single finished sheet lies on a low table under a brush and an ink stone, still blank. No people. Historically accurate: no printed or written characters anywhere, no bound books, no scrolls on rollers. The drying sheets fill the upper half. Keep the top left corner plain wall and sky.
cards.check: The search corrected the first draft: paper was in Muslim Spain by the 900s.

links.napoleon>rosetta: Soldiers of the army Napoleon took to Egypt found the Rosetta Stone in 1799, built into an old wall they were pulling down.

cards.tx: Draw one more card each turn.
cards.fact: The same decree is carved on it three times: in hieroglyphs, in the everyday script of Egypt and in Greek. Scholars could read the Greek, and that was their way in to the other two.
cards.art: The Rosetta Stone as it was found in July 1799, half dug out of the rubble of an old fort wall in the Nile delta: a slab of dark grey stone about as tall as a child of ten, its top corners and one lower corner broken away, standing tilted in a trench of sand and broken brick. Its polished face is covered from top to bottom with fine carved writing in three bands that are plainly different from each other: small pictures at the top, a flowing script in the middle, and neat square letters at the bottom. A soldier's pick and a wooden measuring rod lean beside it, and a hand has just brushed the dust from the middle band. Hard sunlight rakes across the carving. No people but the one hand. Historically accurate: no writing that can be read, no gold, no pyramids behind. The stone stands in the upper half, right of centre. Keep the top left corner sky and wall.

cards.tx: Your Figures can walk two steps.
cards.fact: At trials near Liverpool in 1829 a locomotive named Rocket ran at about thirty miles an hour, a speed no horse could keep up for long. Within twenty years Britain had laid some six thousand miles of railway.
cards.art: The locomotive Rocket at speed in October 1829: a small engine painted bright yellow with black bands, with a tall thin white chimney at the front, a short barrel of a boiler, two big spoked driving wheels turned by cylinders set at a slant on each side, and a pair of small wheels behind, pulling a four-wheeled tender that carries a water barrel. It rushes from left to right along a plain iron track on a low embankment, white steam streaming back flat from the chimney, the driver and fireman small dark figures on the footplate, one holding his hat on. A line of spectators stands far back along a rope with a marquee and flags. Seen from the trackside, low, the engine in the upper half, right of centre. Historically accurate: no cab roof, no cowcatcher, no headlamp, no later streamlining. Keep the top left corner sky and steam.

cards.tx: Once a turn, jump one of your Figures to any Place. It is done for the turn.
cards.fact: The first passengers in a hot-air balloon, sent up before the king of France in 1783, were a sheep, a duck and a rooster. Two months later two men flew across Paris for about twenty-five minutes, feeding a fire of straw beneath the paper-lined bag as they went.
cards.art: The balloon of the Montgolfier brothers on 21 November 1783, floating over the roofs of Paris with the first two people ever to fly: a huge pear-shaped bag of cloth and paper painted deep blue and gold, decorated with suns, swags of drapery and the signs of the zodiac, taller than a church. Around its open neck runs a narrow wicker gallery, and in it, on opposite sides to balance it, stand two tiny men in coats and hats, one waving his hat and the other pushing a forkful of straw into an iron fire basket that hangs in the opening. A thread of smoke trails away. Below lie grey slate roofs, church towers and the river with its bridges, and small crowds on every roof and quay looking up. Seen from the air a little below the balloon, which fills the upper half, right of centre. Historically accurate: no gas burner, no hanging basket on ropes, no modern bright stripes. Keep the top left corner clear sky.

cards.tx: Once a turn, jump one of your Figures to any Place. It is done for the turn.
cards.fact: On 17 December 1903 two bicycle makers from Ohio, Orville and Wilbur Wright, made the first flights in a powered aeroplane. The first lasted twelve seconds and covered less ground than the wingspan of a modern airliner.
cards.art: The Wright brothers' aeroplane on the morning of 17 December 1903 at the instant it leaves the ground: a frail machine of spruce and pale cloth with two long wings one above the other, a pair of small flat surfaces held out in front on struts, a double rudder behind, and two slow wooden propellers at the back driven by chains. It has just lifted a hand's breadth off the end of a single wooden rail laid on flat sand. One man lies face down on the lower wing with his hips in a cradle and his hands on a lever; the other, in a dark suit and cap, has let go of the wing tip and stands frozen in mid-stride, watching. A low bench and a coil of wire lie on the sand. Cold grey light, wind off the sea, a big dune behind. Seen from behind and to the right, the machine in the upper half, right of centre. Historically accurate: no wheels, no seat, no enclosed body, no engine cowling. Keep the top left corner blank winter sky.
cards.check: The flights were at Kill Devil Hills, four miles from Kitty Hawk.

links.washington>delaware: Washington led his army across the Delaware River on Christmas night of 1776 and took the town of Trenton by surprise in the morning.

cards.tx: One of your Figures clashes with an enemy at its Place with +1 Might, even if it has already acted.
cards.fact: On Christmas night of 1776 Washington took 2,400 men, with their horses and eighteen cannon, across a river full of floating ice in the dark. They marched nine miles through a storm of sleet and surprised the enemy garrison at Trenton soon after dawn.
cards.art: The crossing of the Delaware River on the night of 25 December 1776, seen as it was and not as the famous painting shows it: black water crowded with slabs of floating ice, and on it several long, heavy, high-sided cargo boats, black, pointed at both ends, each packed with standing soldiers wrapped in blankets and poled and rowed by boatmen who fend off the ice with boat hooks. Beyond them a flat ferry carries two frightened horses and the barrel and wheels of a cannon. Sleet drives across from the right. On the near bank a few lanterns show men in ragged coats, some with rags tied around their feet, hauling on a rope. Nobody stands heroically in a bow and no flag flies. Seen from the bank, the boats in the upper half of the picture. Historically accurate: night, not dawn; no small rowing boat, no stars and stripes. Keep the top left corner darkness and sleet.
cards.check: The eighteen cannon were not returned. Counts of the men vary; 2,400 is the usual figure for Washington's own column.

links.arminius>teutoburg: Arminius led three Roman legions into the Teutoburg Forest in AD 9 and destroyed them there.

cards.tx: One of your Figures clashes with an enemy at its Place with +1 Might, even if it has already acted.
cards.fact: In AD 9 three Roman legions were strung out along a narrow track between a wooded hill and a bog, in the rain, when Arminius's warriors struck from behind a wall of turf. Traces of that wall and thousands of lost Roman things have been dug up at Kalkriese in Germany.
cards.art: The ambush in the Teutoburg Forest in September of AD 9: a narrow, muddy track running between a steep wooded slope on the left and a reedy bog on the right, in heavy rain. Along the track a Roman column has stopped in confusion, soldiers in mail and strip armour with their big curved shields still in leather rain covers, baggage mules, a bogged cart. Along the foot of the slope runs a low wall of cut turf topped with wattle, and over it and through gaps in it Germanic warriors with long narrow shields and spears are pouring down onto the track. In the mud in the foreground lies a Roman cavalryman's face mask of silvered iron, fallen and staring up, rain beading on it. Seen from low on the track, the fight in the upper half and middle distance, the mask at the lower right. No horned or winged helmets, no close view of wounds. Keep the top left corner dark wet branches.

links.caesar>testudo: In his own account of invading Britain, Caesar tells how the Seventh Legion locked shields into a tortoise to storm a stronghold in the woods.

cards.tx: Quick. One of your Figures gets +2 Might for one clash. On the other player's turn it plays itself when it would save your Figure, paid for with 1 Spark you kept.
cards.fact: Testudo is Latin for tortoise. Roman soldiers locked their shields edge to edge in front, at the sides and over their heads, and walked up to an enemy wall under a rain of arrows and stones.
cards.art: A Roman tortoise of shields about 54 BC, seen from the wall it is attacking, looking down: a tight block of some thirty soldiers has become a single roof of long oval shields, overlapping like tiles, with a wall of shields along the front and sides and only sandalled feet and the tips of a few short swords showing at the edges. Stones and javelins thrown from above are bouncing off the shield roof, one in mid-air, and a clay pot has just smashed across it. The block moves steadily up a ramp of piled brushwood toward us. Behind it more soldiers wait in the open under an eagle standard. Every shield carries the same painted pattern. Seen from above and in front, the formation in the middle and upper half of the picture. The late Roman Republic: oval shields curved like a section of barrel, mail shirts, plain bronze helmets; no rectangular shields, no segmented plate. Keep the top left corner earth bank and sky.
cards.check: Caesar, Gallic War 5.9.

links.douglass>brownsbox: Frederick Douglass wished Henry Brown's escape in a box had been kept quiet, so that others could have got away by the same road.

cards.tx: A Figure costing 3 or less arrives from your hand at any Place.
cards.fact: In 1849 Henry Brown, enslaved in Virginia, had himself nailed into a wooden box about three feet long and sent by express to Philadelphia. He travelled twenty-seven hours by wagon, train and steamboat, part of the way upside down, and stepped out a free man.
cards.art: Henry Brown's box on its way north in March 1849: a plain crate of rough boards, about three feet long and two wide, bound with five hoops of hickory, standing among trunks, mail sacks and barrels in the dim baggage car of a moving train. A paper label is pasted on its lid, and three small holes are bored in one end. Two railway porters in caps and aprons are sitting on it, one at each end, sharing a pipe, with no idea what is under them. A swinging lantern lights the car; through the half-open sliding door the night country streams past. In one of the three small holes, if one looks closely, a little lamplight catches the white of an eye. Seen from across the car, the crate in the middle of the picture and the porters' heads in the upper half. Historically accurate: no bars, no chains, no lettering that can be read. Keep the top left corner dark roof of the car.
cards.check: That he travelled part of the way upside down was not returned.

cards.tx: Jump one of your Figures to any Place. It is done for the turn.
cards.fact: Polynesian navigators crossed thousands of miles of open Pacific without instruments, steering by the stars, the swells and the flight of birds. In 1976 the canoe Hōkūle‘a showed that it could be done by sailing from Hawaii to Tahiti in the old way.
cards.art: A Polynesian voyaging canoe far out on the open Pacific about a thousand years ago, just after sunset: two long slender hulls joined side by side by a platform of lashed poles, with a small thatched shelter on it, driven by two tall sails shaped like a crab's claw, woven of pale matting. The canoe rides up the face of a long ocean swell. In the stern the navigator stands braced at a great steering paddle, an older man in a wrapped bark-cloth garment, his face lifted to the first bright star low on the horizon ahead, while two white sea birds fly the same way overhead, homing to land. The crew, men and women, sit among baskets, gourds of water, a pig and young plants wrapped in leaves. Seen from the water astern and to one side, the sails and the star in the upper half. Historically accurate: two hulls, not one hull with a float; no carved tiki figurehead, no flower garlands, no compass. Keep the top left corner darkening sky.

links.douglass>railroad: Frederick Douglass hid people escaping slavery in his own house in Rochester, and sent them on to Canada.

cards.tx: Jump one of your Figures to any Place. It is done for the turn.
cards.fact: It was neither underground nor a railroad, but a secret chain of people and safe houses that helped men, women and children escape slavery and reach the free states and Canada. Its guides were called conductors and its hiding places stations.
cards.art: A station on the Underground Railroad on a winter night about 1850: the back of a plain white farmhouse in the northern United States, snow on the ground, a single lamp set in an upstairs window. In the yard a farm wagon stands loaded high with sacks of grain, and its driver, a farmer in a broad hat and greatcoat, is lifting two of the sacks aside to show a hidden space between them. Out of it a Black man is helping a woman who carries a sleeping child, both wrapped in blankets and stiff with cold. A woman from the house holds the kitchen door open on a bar of yellow light, a quilt over her arm, and looks past them down the dark lane to be sure nobody has followed. Bare trees, a barn, the Big Dipper above the roof. Seen from the lane, the house and the lit window in the upper half. No chains, no dogs or pursuers in the picture. Keep the top left corner night sky.

links.darwin>beagle: Charles Darwin sailed as naturalist on HMS Beagle, and filled the ship with the rocks, bones and animals he collected.

cards.tx: Draw 2 cards.
cards.fact: HMS Beagle was a small survey ship, only about ninety feet long, sent to chart the coasts of South America. Her voyage was meant to take two years and lasted almost five.
cards.art: HMS Beagle in 1834, lying at anchor in a narrow channel at the far southern tip of South America: a small, sturdy wooden ship with three masts, her sails furled, a white band along her dark hull and boats slung at her sides and stern. She is dwarfed by what stands behind her: a wall of dark beech forest rising straight from the water, and above it a great mountain of blue ice and snow whose glacier comes down to the sea. One of the ship's boats is pulling for the shore with a few men and a pile of boxes and nets. On the cramped deck and hanging in the rigging, small but plain to see, are the collector's things: crates, glass jars, a net, bones laid out to dry. Cold clear light, seabirds, a whale's back in the channel. Seen from the water, the ship in the middle and the mountain in the upper half. Historically accurate: no steam funnel, no gun smoke. Keep the top left corner cloud on the mountain.
cards.check: Not returned by the search. The ship's length (90 feet) and the two years planned are standard, written from memory.

links.harun>wisdom: The caliphs' great library in Baghdad, the House of Wisdom, is said to have begun as the book collection of Harun al-Rashid.
links.alkhwarizmi>wisdom: Al-Khwarizmi worked at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad under Harun's son, the caliph al-Ma'mun.

cards.tx: Draw 2 cards.
cards.fact: In ninth-century Baghdad the caliphs paid scholars of many faiths to gather the books of Greece, Persia and India and put them into Arabic. Some works of Greek science survive today only in those translations.
cards.art: A translator's table in Baghdad about the year 830: a low desk seen close, on which two books lie open side by side. The one on the left is old and worn, a Greek book of geometry with diagrams of circles and triangles and writing in angular letters; the one on the right is new, the same diagrams freshly redrawn in red and black with flowing writing that runs from right to left, the ink of the last line still wet. Between them two hands meet over the page: an older scholar's finger rests on a line of the Greek, and a younger man's hand holds a reed pen ready above the Arabic. An inkwell, a pen knife, a pair of dividers and a third book with Indian numerals lie at the edges. Behind, out of focus, a hall with niches full of books laid flat and other scholars at their desks. Only hands and sleeves, no faces. No writing that can be read. The books fill the middle of the picture. Keep the top left corner dim arches.
cards.check: That al-Khwarizmi worked there was not returned. Sources date the library's start to Harun's reign or to 825.

links.magellan>galleon: The galleons sailed to the Philippines, the islands that Magellan had reached for Spain in 1521.

cards.tx: Gain 3 Spark.
cards.fact: For 250 years, from 1565, great ships sailed once or twice a year between Manila and Acapulco, carrying American silver west and Chinese silk and porcelain east. The voyage to Mexico took four months or more, one of the longest regular crossings of its time.
cards.art: A Manila galleon being loaded in Manila Bay about 1600 for the crossing to Mexico: a very large, high-sided wooden ship with a tall carved stern, three masts and furled sails, riding at anchor. Around her crowd the craft that feed her: Chinese junks with ribbed matting sails, from which bales of raw silk and straw-packed crates of blue-and-white porcelain are being swung aboard on ropes, and small outrigger boats bringing water jars, rice and chickens. On the galleon's deck an officer checks a list beside an open chest heaped with silver coins. Beyond lie the stone walls of the city, palm trees and green mountains under towering cloud. Seen from a small boat alongside, the galleon's side and stern rising through the upper half of the picture. Historically accurate: no gunfire, no skull flag, no steam. Keep the top left corner cloud and sky.
cards.check: The search corrected the first draft: the crossing to Mexico is given as four months, not six.

cards.tx: Gain 3 Spark.
cards.fact: Gold was found at a sawmill in California in January 1848. Within two years about a hundred thousand people had come by wagon and by ship, from as far away as Chile, China and Australia.
cards.art: A miner's pan in a California river in 1849, seen close from above: a wide, shallow iron pan held tilted in two wet, cracked hands just under the surface of clear fast water, with a crescent of black sand left along its lower edge, and in the black sand a scatter of bright yellow flakes and one small nugget. The water swirling out of the pan carries away the pale gravel. Around the hands are river stones, a pick, a worn boot planted in the stream. In the upper half of the picture the river runs away up a canyon lined with other diggers at wooden rocker boxes and sluices, canvas tents, a mule, pine trees and smoke: people in every kind of dress, a Chinese miner in a wide hat, a Chilean in a poncho, a sailor. Hard mountain light. No faces close up. Historically accurate: no machinery, no town. Keep the top left corner pines and sky.

cards.fact: On Christmas Eve of 1914, in the first winter of the First World War, soldiers in the trenches of both sides began singing carols across the lines. In many places they climbed out next day to shake hands, swap small gifts and bury their dead, and here and there kicked a football about.
cards.art: Christmas morning of 1914 between the trenches in Flanders: a flat field white with frost under a pale sun, crossed by two tangles of barbed wire. Out in the middle, in twos and threes, soldiers of both armies stand together, their rifles left behind: men in khaki greatcoats and soft caps, and men in grey with round caps or spiked helmets with cloth covers. At the centre one of each is shaking hands; beside them two more are trading a tin and a handful of cigars, and one soldier has put on the other's helmet and is being laughed at. Along the parapet of the farther trench stands a row of tiny fir trees with candles. Others are climbing out, hands empty and held up. Breath smokes in the cold. Seen from the lip of the nearer trench, the meeting in the middle of the picture. No fighting, no bodies, no tanks. Keep the top left corner pale winter sky.
cards.check: Not returned by the search. Standard, written from memory.

links.eleanor>magnacarta: King John, who was made to put his seal to Magna Carta in 1215, was Eleanor of Aquitaine's youngest son.

cards.tx: Enemy Figures at one Place miss their next turn.
cards.fact: In 1215 the barons of England forced King John to put his seal to a long list of promises, among them that no free man would be jailed except by the law of the land. Four copies written out that summer still exist.
cards.art: The sealing of Magna Carta in a meadow beside the Thames in June 1215, seen close across a table: a single large sheet of parchment covered edge to edge with small, close writing lies on a cloth, and a clerk's hands are pressing a lump of soft green wax, hung from the foot of the sheet on a cord, between the two halves of a great seal press. Around the table stand the people who matter, cut off at the chest so that we see only hands and belts: on one side several men in mail with their gloved hands resting on their sword hilts, on the other a hand heavy with rings that grips the table's edge, and between them a bishop's hand raised to keep the peace. Grass, a striped tent pole, river light. No faces. Historically accurate: the king does not sign with a pen, no crown on the table, no writing that can be read. The parchment and the seal are in the middle of the picture. Keep the top left corner tent cloth.
cards.check: The sealing at Runnymede and the four copies were confirmed. The search did not return the wording of the clause or that John was Eleanor's youngest son; both are standard.

links.aeschylus>marathonmarch: Aeschylus fought in the Athenian line at Marathon, where his brother was killed.

cards.fact: After beating the Persians on the beach at Marathon in 490 BC, the Athenians saw the enemy fleet put to sea and make for their undefended city. They hurried the twenty-five miles home, and were waiting above the shore when the ships arrived.
cards.art: The Athenian army after the battle of Marathon in 490 BC, hurrying home to save its city: a long column of tired Greek foot soldiers coming toward us along a dusty coast road between pines, bronze helmets pushed back on their heads, big round shields slung on their backs, long spears on their shoulders, many bandaged, all of them grey with dust and sweat and none of them stopping. The nearest man drinks from a skin as he walks; another has his arm around a limping friend. Out on the bright sea to the right, level with the head of the column and going the same way, a line of dark ships under oar and sail is racing them along the coast. The sun is low. Seen from the road ahead of the column, the leading soldiers from the knees up in the middle of the picture, the ships in the upper right. Greece in 490 BC: no lone runner collapsing, no capes, no letters on the shields. Keep the top left corner pine branches.
cards.check: Herodotus 6.116. The search corrected the first draft: some scholars put the march on the day after the battle.

links.beethoven>ninth: The Ode to Joy is the last movement of Beethoven's Ninth Symphony, first played in Vienna in 1824.

cards.fact: At the first performance of his Ninth Symphony in 1824, Beethoven stood beside the conductor beating time, too deaf to hear the orchestra or the cheering. One of the singers turned him around by the sleeve so that he could see the audience on its feet.
cards.art: The end of the first performance of the Ninth Symphony, in a theatre in Vienna on 7 May 1824, seen from the back of the stage: in the middle, with his back to the hall, stands a stocky grey-haired man in a dark green coat, still bent over a score on a stand and still beating time with one hand, though the music has stopped. A young woman, one of the solo singers, in a pale high-waisted gown, has stepped up beside him and taken his sleeve in her fingers, and is gently turning him by the arm to face the house. Past them, over the footlights, the whole audience is standing, tier above tier of boxes, waving hats and white handkerchiefs in the air so that he can see the applause he cannot hear. Players of the orchestra have lowered their bows and are watching him. Seen from among the choir, the two figures from the knees up in the middle, the hall blazing in the upper half. No piano, no laurel wreath. Keep the top left corner dark stage curtain.

links.gandhi>saltmarch: Gandhi led the march to the sea at Dandi in 1930 and made salt there in defiance of the law.

cards.fact: It began with Gandhi and 78 companions and took 24 days. By the time they reached the sea the line of walkers was about two miles long, and within the year some sixty thousand people had gone to jail for making or selling salt.
cards.art: The Salt March in March 1930, seen from a rise beside the road: a dusty country road in western India running away across flat fields to the horizon, and on it a column of walkers so long that its tail is lost in the haze, almost all of them in white homespun, with white caps, some carrying bundles on their heads. At the head, small in the picture, a thin figure in a short white wrap strides out fast with a tall bamboo staff, and those behind are having to hurry to keep up. Villagers have swept the road and sprinkled it with water and stand along both sides with garlands and brass pots; boys have climbed a banyan tree to see. Morning sun, long shadows, a glint of sea far ahead. Seen from above and in front, the column running from the upper left distance down to the lower right. No soldiers, no flags, no faces close up. Keep the top left corner haze and sky.

links.douglass>emancipation: Frederick Douglass went to the White House in 1863 and again in 1864 to speak to Lincoln for the Black soldiers the Proclamation had brought into the army.

cards.fact: From 1 January 1863 it declared free the people held as slaves in the states at war with the Union, and opened the army and navy to Black men. Nearly two hundred thousand of them served before the war ended.
cards.art: Watch Night, 31 December 1862, in a small wooden church in the American South, a few minutes before midnight: a congregation of Black men, women and children, most of them enslaved, crowded on plain benches and standing along the walls, every face turned toward the front. There an old man with white hair stands holding up a large silver pocket watch by its chain in the light of a single torch, and beside him a boy has his hand raised, counting. Some are praying with their eyes shut and hands clasped, a mother holds a baby up to see, a young man in a soldier's blue coat stands at the door. On the wall hangs a printed notice. All the light comes from the torch, gold on their faces against the dark. Seen from the back of the church, the watch and the old man in the upper half, right of centre. No chains, no overseer, no writing that can be read. Keep the top left corner dark rafters.

merge: Relics and Deeds: engine.js names each Relic and Deed by its key ('compass', 'press', 'antikythera', 'eureka', 'caravan', 'decree', 'eclipse', 'encore', 'fairwinds', 'ambush', 'trojan', 'phalanx'). Every new Relic and Deed here has `as`: the existing card whose effect, cost and rules text it takes. To play them, the engine (and the EV handlers in ui.js that name those keys) must look up `CARDS[key].as || key` where it now compares the key. Two Relics with the same `as` do the same thing, so a player should not be able to have both in play (hasRelic should compare `as`).

Eras: cards.js has six eras and the last, The Age of Steam, ends in 1900. Ten Figures here have a year after 1900 (Einstein, Turing, Gandhi, Martin Luther King Jr., Mandela, Jim Thorpe, Jesse Owens, Frida Kahlo, Houdini, Amelia Earhart), and so do the Wright Flyer, the Christmas Truce and the Salt March. The Figures are given era 6, the only value cards.js knows, and the Library would file them under 1800 to 1900. A seventh era is needed before they go in, for example { n: 'The Modern Age', to: 2000 }.
